'''James Lee Fergason'''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.publicrecords.com/people-search-records/james-fergason|title=James Fergason public records|publisher=Public Records.com|year=2013|accessdate=October 11, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131012014800/http://www.publicrecords.com/people-search-records/james-fergason|archive-date=October 12, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> (January 12, 1934 – December 9, 2008) was an [[United States of America|American]] inventor and business entrepreneur. A member of the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]], Fergason is best known for his work on an improved [[liquid crystal display]], or LCD. He held over one hundred U.S. patents at the time of his death.<ref name=SPIE>{{cite web|url=http://spie.org/x32291.xml|title=In Memoriam - James L. Fergason|publisher=SPIE.org|year=2013|accessdate=October 11, 2013}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
James Lee "Jim" Fergason was born on a farm near the small town of [[Wakenda, Missouri|Wakenda, Carroll County, Missouri]].<ref name=Legends>{{cite book|last=Brown|first=John W.|title=Missouri Legends: Famous people from the Show-Me State|year=2008|publisher=Reedy Press|pages=107–08|location=St. Louis}}</ref>

He was educated in a one-room schoolhouse until the 7th grade when his family moved to the county seat of [[Carrollton, Missouri|Carrollton]]. The Fergason family had something of a reputation for educational over achievement. One grandfather graduated from college at age fifteen, while two of Fergason's older brothers studied chemical engineering and electrical engineering respectively. A cousin was an agricultural engineer who had over 100 patents for his machinery inventions.<ref name=Lemelson>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/invent/a-winners/a-fergason.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060919153814/http://web.mit.edu/invent/a-winners/a-fergason.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 19, 2006|title=James Fergason - 2006 Lemelson-MIT Prize Winner|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology via website|year=2013|accessdate=October 10, 2013}}</ref>

Following his graduation from Carrollton High School in 1952 he enrolled at the [[University of Missouri]], earning a [[Bachelor's Degree]] in [[physics]] in 1956. Fergason married his wife Dora the week after graduation from Mizzou, then reported for a brief tour of duty as a second lieutenant with the [[United States Army]] in [[Texas]].<ref name=Legends/>

==Professional career==
After his discharge from the Army, Fergason was hired by Westinghouse Research Laboratories in [[Pennsylvania]]. At Westinghouse he began groundbreaking work with cholesteric liquid crystals, forming the first industrial research group into the practical uses of the technology. For this work Fergason earned his first [[patent]] ({{US patent|3114836}}) in 1963. Among the later uses for his research and first patent were the 1970s pop culture icon the [[mood ring]], and the [[Liquid crystal thermometer]].<ref name=Youtube>{{cite video|people=James L. Fergason|title=James L. Fergason, 2006 Lemelson-MIT prize winner |medium=video interview|publisher=The Lemelson Foundation|year=2006|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=It1AtTcpQhc |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211219/It1AtTcpQhc |archive-date=2021-12-19 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In June 1966, Fergason joined the [[Liquid Crystal Institute]] at [[Kent State University]] as its associate director. Here, in 1969, he made his seminal discovery of a low-power, field-operated liquid crystal display, known as the [[twisted nematic]] cell, and received a patent.({{US patent|3731986}})<ref>Patent US3731986: ''Display devices utilizing liquid crystal light modification.'' Filed on 22 April 1971, published 8 May 1973. Inventor: James L. Fergason.</ref> There was a controversy about this invention. The inventors [[Martin Schadt]] and [[Wolfgang Helfrich]]<ref>[https://ethw.org/Wolfgang_Helfrich ''Wolfgang Helfrich.''] Engineering and Technology History Wiki. Retrieved 27 May 2020.</ref> of [[Hoffmann-La Roche]] had filed a Swiss patent application for the same invention at an earlier international priority date than Fergason in 1970.<ref>Patent CH532261: ''Lichtsteuerzelle.'' Filed on 4 December 1970, published on 31 December 1972. Inventors: Wolfgang Helfrich, Martin Schadt.</ref> However, a US patent was granted to Fergason due to a predated US patent notebook entry in 1970. All three were awarded the [[IEEE Jun-ichi Nishizawa Medal]] in 2008 for this invention. Also at LCI, Fergason was part of an effort to use [[cholesteric]] liquid crystals for thermal mapping, in particular, to screen for [[breast cancer]]. He participated in the discovery of [[smectic]] C liquid crystal phase.<ref name=Legends/><ref name="OSA"/>

Twisted nematic liquid crystal displays were superior to the earlier [[dynamic scattering]] displays, and soon became widespread.  The technology was patented in the United States by Fergason in 1971. He formed his own company, ILIXCO, in 1968 to manufacture liquid crystal displays. His first customers were the Bulova Watch Company and Gruen Watch Company which used the technology to market the first LCD watches using this technology. By the end of the decade, most of the world's digital watches used this kind of LCD. Fergason held over 150 patents in the United States and over 500 foreign patents. He also was inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]]. In 2001, he founded '''Fergason Patent Properties''', which managed licensing of his patents.<ref name=Legends/><ref name="OSA"/>

In 2001, he was awarded an honorary doctorate from the [[University of Missouri]], in 2006 he was the recipient of the [[Lemelson-MIT Prize]], in 2007 he was awarded the [[David Richardson Medal]] by the [[Optical Society of America]],<ref name="OSA">{{cite web|url=http://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/awards/award_description/davidrichardson|title=David Richardson Medal|work=OSA.org|publisher=The Optical Society|year=2013|accessdate=December 18, 2013}}</ref> and in 2008 he received the [[IEEE Jun-ichi Nishizawa Medal|Jun-Ichi Nishizawa Medal]] from the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]].<ref name=Legends/><ref name="OSA"/> He was also elected a Fellow of the Optical Society in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James L. Fergason {{!}} Optica |url=https://www.optica.org/about/newsroom/obituaries/earlier/james_l_fergason/ |access-date=2024-09-06 |website=www.optica.org}}</ref> 

==Death==
Fergason died at age 74 in [[Menlo Park, California|Menlo Park]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Obituary: James L. Fergason, pioneer in liquid crystal displays |url=https://www.almanacnews.com/news/2008/12/30/obituary-james-l-fergason-pioneer-in-liquid-crystal-displays/ |access-date=28 December 2024 |work=The Almanac |publisher=almanacnews.com |date=December 30, 2008}}</ref> He was survived by his wife Dora and their four children, Teresa, Jeffrey, John and Susan, and his 11 grandchildren.<ref name=Mercury/><ref name=SPIE/>
